description: Dr Amandeep Hansra: Chief Clinical Adviser, Australian Digital Health Agency; medical repatriation and aviation medicine experience. Mark Hallam: aerospace engineer, ATC project manager; leads our build. A/Prof Eugene Wong: retrieval doctor; Deputy Director, QLD Virtual Emergency Care Service. Dr Raymond Wen: Medical Director, Telecare Australia; designs and delivers life-saving remote models of care, an Earth analogue for space medicine. Arki Prasad: aspiring astronaut and crew physician.
summary: S.E.R.E.N. Clinical helps an astronaut who is not a medical expert act in the gap before Earth can answer: on the way to Mars, a question to Earth's doctors can take up to 45 minutes to come back. It tracks 15 health indicators in seven body systems against each crew member's own baseline and sourced NASA limits, and sorts every result into three tiers: Nothing to do (green circle), Watch (amber triangle) and Act now (red square). Every result explains itself, with its NASA hazard and sources. When something feels wrong, it matches symptom patterns, guides tests such as a urine strip and guided ultrasound, gives the steps to start now and sends a clinical handover to Earth with a countdown to the reply. Possible sepsis or shock opens an emergency mode with 16 voice-guided checklists. The crew can talk to it: it asks each question aloud, reads the answer back and fills the form. Optional AI connections, tested with Google's open Gemma 4 E2B and E4B models running locally with no cloud, fill whole forms from one sentence and suggest the right emergency checklist, while fixed, clinician-signed rules decide every alert. It runs offline with no server, and the same case runs at a Simpson Desert station 640 km from the nearest hospital: space medicine is remote medicine with a longer delay
details:
The problem. On the ISS, help is a radio call away. On the way to Mars, a question to Earth's doctors can take up to 45 minutes to come back, and there is no evacuation. Crews will have to notice changes in themselves, decide and act before a doctor can answer. Our team of GPs, a retrieval and emergency physician, an aerospace engineer and an aspiring astronaut built S.E.R.E.N. Clinical for that gap. It is an assessment and next-steps tool: it never diagnoses.

What it monitors. Fifteen indicators in seven groups: mind and sleep (sleep, mood, reaction time), heart (resting heart rate, blood pressure), eyes (a visual acuity self-check), muscle and bone (exercise plan done, grip strength, body mass), food and fluid, blood (haemoglobin), and cabin and radiation (cabin carbon dioxide, radiation dose). Most are compared with the person's own baseline; some also have a sourced NASA limit, such as grip strength at 80% of baseline and the 600 mSv career radiation limit. Drift alerts catch slow change away from a person's usual vital signs. A one-screen daily check-in takes under a minute, a scheduler never asks during critical work such as a spacewalk, and an honest-reporting loop counts check-ins, never results. Eight body areas list the symptoms to report and record-only results (such as an ECG or pain score) that travel with a case but are never scored until a clinician writes a rule.

How it decides. Every result lands in one of three tiers, each a colour, a shape and a word: Nothing to do (green circle), Watch (amber triangle), Act now (red square). Emergency is a mode opened from an Act now alert, not a tier. Every result has an explanation card: how to measure, why it matters, what to do, the NASA hazards and the sources. The screens follow NASA's published criteria for crew displays, including 7:1 text contrast and a second cue beside every colour.

The demo story. Jo is on Day 214 at a Mars base, 18 light-minutes from Earth. Three days of low fluid raise a Watch that names kidney stone risk, with NASA's evidence report as its source. Then pain starts: three taps on "Feeling off?", and the matched pattern turns Act now, with steps that include a urine test strip and a guided ultrasound (with drawings, keeping no image and never saying what an image means). A clinical handover goes to Earth and a countdown shows no answer can arrive for 36 minutes, so the crew starts the steps; the doctor's reply lands as a step. Later, fever with low blood pressure or fast breathing raises a possible-sepsis alert that opens emergency mode. In a second thread, Jo's sleep has slid for three weeks while cabin carbon dioxide reached 3.4 mmHg, above NASA's 3 mmHg limit: the app treats the air first, asks for a reaction-time check and shows the signals together. Then the same case runs for Sam, a station hand at a Simpson Desert station 640 km from the nearest hospital.

Emergencies. An Emergency button sits on every screen. ASTRA, the team's emergency module, holds 16 checklists adapted from NASA's Medical Checklist (JSC-48031); a cardiac arrest hands over to guided CPR steps and back. "Say what is happening" turns one spoken sentence into a suggested checklist, shown as a button so nothing opens by itself. A solar radiation storm raises a shelter alarm with a banner until the all-clear.

Places and conditions. Location profiles (Mars base, in transit, Moon base, space station, remote Australia) change the reply delay, guidance, gravity, cabin atmosphere and how far help is. The rules themselves stay the same everywhere.

Voice and devices. On the daily check-in and vital signs, the app asks each question aloud, takes down the spoken answer, reads it back and fills the form. Vital signs can come from a simulated crew device kit or a real Bluetooth device using the published health formats.

Ready for AI, safely. After feedback from judges, we designed the app to be voice-first, with an AI model turning what the crew say into the app's answers, vital signs and checklist commands. We have deliberately submitted it without a model connected: our code is in a public GitHub repository, and an AI service key there would be exposed and could run up costs. Instead, the app is built ready to connect to one. A cloud language model, an on-device edge model such as Google's Gemma 4 E4B (which can take speech directly and runs offline), or a larger open-weight frontier model can be plugged in without changing the clinical rules. For a real Mars mission, on-device is the only option, because a cloud service is 18 minutes away. Whatever model is used, it only fills in inputs; the rules decide, and our design reads every value back for the crew to confirm.

Optional AI connections, tested on real open models. Off by default, and set up in the app's settings with any OpenAI-compatible server (for example Ollama or llama.cpp). Three uses: a small language model fills whole forms, symptoms and vital signs from one natural sentence; it suggests which emergency checklist fits; and an AI clinical assistant answers when Earth can't, using a cloud model where Earth is within a minute (low Earth orbit to the Moon) or a model on a computer at the location. The cloud option is refused on Mars, with the reason. We tested the app's own AI code against Google's Gemma 4 E2B and E4B (Apache 2.0) running through llama.cpp on four CPU cores with no graphics card. E2B filled all six check-in fields from one sentence in 12 seconds and all six vital signs in 9 seconds. Testing found real problems, which we fixed: a more forgiving reader for loosely formatted replies, clearer instructions for spoken numbers, a red-flag phrase safety net for thoughts of self-harm, cardiac arrest always winning on keywords, no emergency suggestions on routine forms, and the assistant being sent the app's active alerts and signed-off first steps and told never to contradict them. Every model reply is checked against the app's own lists and ranges, read back, and saved only when the crew taps save. Keys stay in the browser and are never in the public repository. The full results are in docs/AI_TEST_REPORT.md.

Clinical safety. Rules decide every tier and alert; no model ever sets one. Every rule shows its source and was signed off by the team's clinicians over four review rounds, and the safety gate (SR-01) passed with every rule signed off. A hazard log, evidence grades and a road-to-flight document set out what real use would need. All crew data is synthetic and labelled. It is a hackathon prototype, not for clinical use, and makes no clinical accuracy claim.

Benefits. Earlier detection, fewer missed warnings, safer decisions while waiting for Earth, and a clear record for the flight surgeon. On Earth, Australians in very remote areas die from potentially avoidable causes at 252 per 100,000 against 88 in major cities (AIHW, 2022 to 2024). Next steps: validate thresholds with flight surgeons and remote clinicians, run the AI on target hardware, and trial with analogue crews.

How it is built. React and TypeScript with Vite; rules in YAML; no server, with data saved in the browser's own database (IndexedDB) so it works with no link to Earth. One action layer serves the screens, a command-line tool and AI agents. Python scripts fetch NASA data and generate the synthetic mission. Automated tests cover the rules engine, the action layer and the AI code. Apache 2.0 licence.
